claim: Supergenes are clusters of linked loci that control variation in complex phenotypes.
source: Supergenes are clusters of linked loci that control variation in complex phenotypes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the introduction that establishes the concept of supergenes.

claim: Some supergenes mediate adaptive polymorphisms that are maintained by frequency- or density-dependent natural selection, as in mimicry in butterflies, self-incompatibility in plants, plumage polymorphisms in birds, and heteromorphic sex chromosomes.
source: Some supergenes mediate adaptive polymorphisms that are maintained by some form of frequency- or density-dependent natural selection, as in, for example, mimicry in butterflies, self-incompatibility in plants, plumage polymorphisms in birds, and heteromorphic sex chromosomes (see Schwander et al., 2014; Thompson and Jiggins, 2014, for review).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review papers by Schwander et al., 2014 and Thompson and Jiggins, 2014.

claim: Some supergenes are maintained by selfish social behaviors that enhance the fitness of carriers at the expense of non-carriers, as in some ant species.
source: Other supergenes are maintained by selfish social behaviors that enhance the fitness of carriers at the expense of non-carriers, as in some ant species (Keller and Ross, 1998; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keller and Ross, 1998 and Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Some supergenes are maintained by their ability to achieve selfish, better-than-Mendelian transmission during gametogenesis, as in meiotic drive complexes found in fungi, insects, and mammals.
source: Still other supergenes are maintained by their ability to achieve selfish, better-than-Mendelian transmission during gametogenesis, as in the so-called meiotic drive complexes found in fungi, insects, and mammals (Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Svedberg et al., 2018; Fuller et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Svedberg et al., 2018; Fuller et al., 2020.

claim: In heterozygous carriers of male drive complexes in animals, the driver disables spermatids that bear drive-sensitive target alleles.
source: In heterozygous carriers of male drive complexes in animals, the driver disables spermatids that bear drive-sensitive target alleles (Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012 and Lindholm et al., 2016.

claim: To spread in the population, the driver must be linked in a cis-arrangement to a drive-resistant (insensitive) target allele.
source: To spread in the population, the driver must be linked in a cis-arrangement to a drive-resistant (insensitive) target allele (Charlesworth and Hartl, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Charlesworth and Hartl, 1978.

claim: Recombination between the driver and target can result in a 'suicide' haplotype that distorts against itself.
source: Recombination between the driver and target can result in a 'suicide' haplotype that distorts against itself (Sandler and Carpenter, 1972; Hartl, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sandler and Carpenter, 1972 and Hartl, 1974.

claim: Epistatic interactions between driver and target lead to selection for modifiers of recombination that tighten linkage, such as chromosomal inversions.
source: These epistatic interactions between driver and target lead to selection for modifiers of recombination that tighten linkage, such as chromosomal inversions (Charlesworth and Hartl, 1978; Schwander et al., 2014; Thompson and Jiggins, 2014; Charlesworth, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Charlesworth and Hartl, 1978; Schwander et al., 2014; Thompson and Jiggins, 2014; Charlesworth, 2016.

claim: Meiotic drive complexes originate from two or more loci with some degree of initial linkage.
source: Like most supergenes (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1975; Turner, 1977), meiotic drive complexes originate from two or more loci with some degree of initial linkage.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1975 and Turner, 1977.

claim: Successful drivers tend to be located in regions of low recombination, such as non-recombining sex chromosomes, centromeric regions, or in chromosomal inversions of autosomes.
source: Successful drivers thus tend to be located in regions of low recombination, such as non-recombining sex chromosomes (Hamilton, 1967; Hurst and Pomiankowski, 1991), centromeric regions, or in chromosomal inversions of autosomes (Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Svedberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hamilton, 1967; Hurst and Pomiankowski, 1991; Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Svedberg et al., 2018.

claim: Due to reduced recombination, the efficacy of natural selection in supergene regions is compromised: deleterious mutations can accumulate, and beneficial ones are more readily lost.
source: Due to reduced recombination, the efficacy of natural selection in these regions is compromised: deleterious mutations can accumulate, and beneficial ones are more readily lost (Muller, 1964; Hill and Robertson, 1968; Felsenstein, 1974; Charlesworth et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Muller, 1964; Hill and Robertson, 1968; Felsenstein, 1974; Charlesworth et al., 2009.

claim: Many meiotic drive complexes are homozygous lethal or sterile.
source: Many meiotic drive complexes are thus homozygous lethal or sterile.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of reduced recombination and compromised selection, following from the previous discussion.

claim: Different drive haplotypes that complement one another may be able to recombine, if only among themselves.
source: Different drive haplotypes that complement one another may be able to recombine, if only among themselves (Dod et al., 2003; Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dod et al., 2003; Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015.

claim: Gene conversion from wildtype chromosomes may ameliorate the genetic load of supergenes.
source: Gene conversion from wildtype chromosomes may also ameliorate the genetic load of supergenes (Uyenoyama, 2005; Wang et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Branco et al., 2018; Stolle et al., 2019; Brelsford et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Uyenoyama, 2005; Wang et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Branco et al., 2018; Stolle et al., 2019; Brelsford et al., 2020.

claim: In heterozygous males, SD disables sperm bearing drive-sensitive wildtype chromosomes via a chromatin condensation defect.
source: In heterozygous males, SD disables sperm bearing drive-sensitive wildtype chromosomes via a chromatin condensation defect (Hartl et al., 1967; Temin et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hartl et al., 1967 and Temin et al., 1991.

claim: SD has two main components: the driver, Segregation Distorter (Sd), is a truncated duplication of the gene RanGAP located in chromosome arm 2L.
source: SD has two main components: the driver, Segregation Distorter (Sd), is a truncated duplication of the gene RanGAP located in chromosome arm 2L (Powers and Ganetzky, 1991; Merrill et al., 1999; Kusano et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Powers and Ganetzky, 1991; Merrill et al., 1999; Kusano et al., 2001.

claim: Previous studies of SD chromosomes have detected linked upward modifiers of drive, including Enhancer of SD (E[SD]) on 2L and several others on 2R.
source: Previous studies of SD chromosomes have detected linked upward modifiers of drive, including Enhancer of SD (E[SD]) on 2L and several others on 2R (Sandler and Hiraizumi, 1960; Miklos, 1972; Ganetzky, 1977; Hiraizumi et al., 1980; Brittnacher and Ganetzky, 1984), but their molecular identities are unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sandler and Hiraizumi, 1960; Miklos, 1972; Ganetzky, 1977; Hiraizumi et al., 1980; Brittnacher and Ganetzky, 1984.

claim: The molecular identities of SD modifiers are unknown.
source: Previous studies of SD chromosomes have detected linked upward modifiers of drive, including Enhancer of SD (E[SD]) on 2L and several others on 2R (Sandler and Hiraizumi, 1960; Miklos, 1972; Ganetzky, 1977; Hiraizumi et al., 1980; Brittnacher and Ganetzky, 1984), but their molecular identities are unknown.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Sd-RanGAP and Rsp straddle the centromere, a region of reduced recombination.
source: Sd-RanGAP and Rsp straddle the centromere, a region of reduced recombination, and some SD chromosomes bear pericentric inversions that presumably further tighten linkage among these loci.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the genomic organization of SD components.

claim: Some SD chromosomes bear pericentric inversions that presumably further tighten linkage among SD loci.
source: Sd-RanGAP and Rsp straddle the centromere, a region of reduced recombination, and some SD chromosomes bear pericentric inversions that presumably further tighten linkage among these loci.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a speculative explanation about function.

claim: In heterozygotes with a pericentric inversion, recombination in the inverted region generates aneuploids and therefore reduced fertility.
source: In heterozygotes with a pericentric inversion, recombination in the inverted region generates aneuploids and therefore reduced fertility, although this effect might be mitigated by strong suppression of recombination (Coyne et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coyne et al., 1993.

claim: Many SD chromosomes bear paracentric inversions on 2R.
source: Many SD chromosomes also bear paracentric inversions on 2R (reviewed in Lyttle, 1991; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review papers by Lyttle, 1991 and Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012.

claim: The strong association of paracentric inversions with SD implies a role for epistatic selection in the evolution of these supergenes.
source: Although recombination between paracentric inversions and the main components of SD is possible, their strong association implies a role for epistatic selection in the evolution of these supergenes (Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012 and is based on inference from the observed association.

claim: SD is present at low population frequencies (<5%) around the world.
source: While SD is present at low population frequencies (<5%) around the world (Temin et al., 1991; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Temin et al., 1991 and Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012.

claim: Sd-RanGAP appears to have originated in sub-Saharan Africa, survived the out-of-Africa bottleneck, and spread to the rest of the world.
source: Sd-RanGAP appears to have originated in sub-Saharan Africa, the ancestral geographic range of D. melanogaster, survived the out-of-Africa bottleneck, and spread to the rest of the world (Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple factors likely contribute to the low frequency of SD in populations: negative selection, insensitive Rsp alleles, and unlinked suppressors.
source: Multiple factors likely contribute to the low frequency of SD in populations: negative selection, insensitive Rsp alleles, and unlinked suppressors (reviewed in Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012.

claim: Two independent longitudinal studies suggest that SD haplotypes can replace each other in populations over short time scales (<30 years).
source: Two independent longitudinal studies suggest that SD haplotypes can replace each other in populations over short time scales (<30 years) (Temin and Kreber, 1981; Brand et al., 2015) without major changes in the overall population frequency of SD (Temin and Kreber, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Temin and Kreber, 1981 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: The predominant SD variant in Africa is SD-Mal, which recently swept across the entire continent.
source: The predominant SD variant in Africa is SD-Mal, which recently swept across the entire continent (Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: SD-Mal has a pair of rare, African-endemic, overlapping paracentric inversions spanning ~40% of 2R: In(2R)51B6–11;55E3–12 and In(2R)44F3–12;54E3–10.
source: SD-Mal has a pair of rare, African-endemic, overlapping paracentric inversions spanning ~40% of 2R:In(2R)51B6–11;55E3–12 and In(2R)44F3–12;54E3–10, hereafter collectively referred to as In(2R)Mal (Aulard et al., 2002; Presgraves et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aulard et al., 2002 and Presgraves et al., 2009.

claim: SD-Mal chromosomes are particularly strong drivers, with ~100% transmission.
source: SD-Mal chromosomes are particularly strong drivers, with ~100% transmission.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about SD-Mal phenotype.

claim: Recombinant chromosomes bearing the Sd-RanGAP duplication from SD-Mal but lacking the inversions do not drive.
source: Notably, recombinant chromosomes bearing the Sd-RanGAP duplication from this haplotype but lacking the inversions do not drive (Presgraves et al., 2009), suggesting that In(2R)Mal is essential for SD-Mal drive.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Presgraves et al., 2009.

claim: In(2R)Mal is essential for SD-Mal drive.
source: Notably, recombinant chromosomes bearing the Sd-RanGAP duplication from this haplotype but lacking the inversions do not drive (Presgraves et al., 2009), suggesting that In(2R)Mal is essential for SD-Mal drive.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that recombinants lacking the inversion do not drive, as cited from Presgraves et al., 2009.

claim: The authors sequenced haploid embryos from nine driving SD-Mal haplotypes sampled from a single population in Zambia.
source: To investigate the evolutionary genomics of SD-Mal, we sequenced haploid embryos from nine driving SD-Mal haplotypes sampled from a single population in Zambia (Brand et al., 2015), the putative ancestral range of D. melanogaster (Pool et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Illumina read depth among samples ranged between ~46 and 67×.
source: Illumina read depth among samples ranged between ~46 and 67× (Supplementary file 1; BioProject PRJNA649752 in NCBI).
evidence: This is a data description from the sequencing results.

claim: The authors obtained ~12× coverage with long-read Nanopore sequencing of one homozygous viable line, SD-ZI125, to create a de novo assembly of a representative SD-Mal haplotype.
source: Additionally, we obtained ~12× coverage with long-read Nanopore sequencing of one homozygous viable line, SD-ZI125, to create a de novo assembly of a representative SD-Mal haplotype (BioProject PRJNA649752 in NCBI; assembly in Navarro-Dominguez et al., 2022a).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for assembly.

claim: All SD-Mal chromosomes have the Sd-RanGAP duplication at the same location as the parent gene on chromosome 2L.
source: All SD-Mal chromosomes have the Sd-RanGAP duplication at the same location as the parent gene on chromosome 2L (see also Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the authors' data and supported by a citation to Brand et al., 2015.

claim: The Rsp locus corresponds to a block of ~120 bp satellite repeats in 2R heterochromatin.
source: The Rsp locus, the target of SD, corresponds to a block of ~120 bp satellite repeats in 2R heterochromatin (Figure 1B; Wu et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 1988 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The reference genome, Iso-1, has a Rsps allele corresponding to a primary Rsp locus containing two blocks of tandem Rsp repeats—Rsp-proximal and Rsp-major—with ~1000 copies of the Rsp satellite repeat interrupted by TEs.
source: The reference genome, Iso-1, has a Rsps allele corresponding to a primary Rsp locus containing two blocks of tandem Rsp repeats—Rsp-proximal and Rsp-major—with ~1000 copies of the Rsp satellite repeat interrupted by TEs (Khost et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khost et al., 2017.

claim: There are three additional Rsp loci in Iso-1 outside of the primary Rsp locus: ~ 10 copies in 2R distal to the major Rsp locus (Rsp-minor); a single copy at the distal end of 2R (60A); and ~12 copies in 3L.
source: There are three of these additional Rsp loci in Iso-1: ~ 10 copies in 2R, distal to the major Rsp locus (Rsp-minor); a single copy at the distal end of 2R (60A); and ~12 copies in 3L (Houtchens and Lyttle, 2003; Larracuente, 2014; Khost et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Houtchens and Lyttle, 2003; Larracuente, 2014; Khost et al., 2017.

claim: The genomes of SD flies carry ~20 copies of Rsp.
source: The genomes of SD flies carry ~20 copies of Rsp (Wu et al., 1988; Pimpinelli and Dimitri, 1989), but the organization of the primary Rsp locus on SD chromosomes is unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 1988 and Pimpinelli and Dimitri, 1989.

claim: All SD-Mal have a complete deletion of the primary Rsp locus containing Rsp-proximal and Rsp-major.
source: This suggests that all SD-Mal have a complete deletion of the primary Rsp locus containing Rsp-proximal and Rsp-major and that the only Rsp copies in the SD-Mal genomes are the minor Rsp loci in chromosomes 2R and 3L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from read mapping data showing very few reads map to Rsp-major in SD-Mal, as shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The only Rsp copies in the SD-Mal genomes are the minor Rsp loci in chromosomes 2R and 3L.
source: This suggests that all SD-Mal have a complete deletion of the primary Rsp locus containing Rsp-proximal and Rsp-major and that the only Rsp copies in the SD-Mal genomes are the minor Rsp loci in chromosomes 2R and 3L (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion of the primary Rsp locus and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distal inversion In(2R)Mal-d occurred first and spanned 4.18 Mb (approx. 2R:14,591,003–18,774,475).
source: From this organization, we infer that the distal inversion, which we refer to as In(2R)Mal-d, occurred first and spanned 4.18 Mb (approx. 2R:14,591,003–18,774,475).
evidence: This is inferred from the assembly data showing the organization of sequence blocks in Figure 1D.

claim: The proximal inversion In(2R)Mal-p occurred second and spanned 6.76 Mb, with 1.02 Mb overlapping with the proximal region of In(2R)Mal-d (approx. 2R:8,855,602–17,749,310).
source: The proximal inversion, which we refer to as In(2R)Mal-p, occurred second and spanned 6.76 Mb, with 1.02 Mb overlapping with the proximal region of In(2R)Mal-d (approx. 2R:8,855,602–17,749,310).
evidence: This is inferred from the assembly data showing the organization of sequence blocks in Figure 1D.

claim: All four breakpoints of the In(2R)Mal rearrangement involve simple joins of unique sequence.
source: All four breakpoints of the In(2R)Mal rearrangement involve simple joins of unique sequence.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the assembly data.

source: Three of these four breakpoints span genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3): sns (2R:8,798,489–8,856,091), CG10931 (2R:17,748,935–17,750,136), and Mctp (2R:18,761,758–18,774,824).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the assembly data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CDSs of both sns and Mctp remain intact in the In(2R)Mal arrangement, with the inversion disrupting their 3' UTRs.
source: The CDSs of both sns and Mctp remain intact in the In(2R)Mal arrangement, with the inversion disrupting their 3' UTRs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the assembly data.

claim: Neither sns nor Mctp is expressed in testes.
source: Neither of these two genes is expressed in testes (https://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0024189; https://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0034389; Chintapalli et al., 2007; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021), making it unlikely that they affect drive.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to FlyBase and Chintapalli et al., 2007; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021.

claim: It is unlikely that sns and Mctp affect drive.
source: Neither of these two genes is expressed in testes (https://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0024189; https://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0034389; Chintapalli et al., 2007; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021), making it unlikely that they affect drive.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of testis expression.

claim: In(2R)Mal-p disrupts the CDS of CG10931, which is a histone methyltransferase with high expression levels in testis.
source: In(2R)Mal-p disrupts the CDS of CG10931, which is a histone methyltransferase with high expression levels in testis (https://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0034274; Chintapalli et al., 2007; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to FlyBase and Chintapalli et al., 2007; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021.

claim: The In(2R)Mal inversion breakpoints disrupt physical domains reported in Hou et al., 2012.
source: The In(2R)Mal inversion breakpoints disrupt physical domains reported in Hou et al., 2012, however inversion-mediated disruptions of TAD boundaries do not necessarily affect gene expression (Ghavi-Helm et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2012 and Ghavi-Helm et al., 2019.

claim: Inversion-mediated disruptions of TAD boundaries do not necessarily affect gene expression.
source: The In(2R)Mal inversion breakpoints disrupt physical domains reported in Hou et al., 2012, however inversion-mediated disruptions of TAD boundaries do not necessarily affect gene expression (Ghavi-Helm et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghavi-Helm et al., 2019.

claim: In African populations, chromosomes bearing Sd but lacking In(2R)Mal do not drive.
source: In African populations, chromosomes bearing Sd but lacking In(2R)Mal do not drive (Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: In(2R)Mal reduces the b–c genetic distance by 54.6% compared with control crosses between b c px and Oregon-R.
source: As expected, In(2R)Mal suppresses recombination: in crosses between a multiply marked chromosome 2, b c px, and SD-Mal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), we find that In(2R)Mal reduces the b–c genetic distance by 54.6% and the c–px genetic distance by 92.4%, compared with control crosses between b c px and Oregon-R (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 1.

claim: In(2R)Mal reduces the c–px genetic distance by 92.4% compared with control crosses between b c px and Oregon-R.
source: As expected, In(2R)Mal suppresses recombination: in crosses between a multiply marked chromosome 2, b c px, and SD-Mal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), we find that In(2R)Mal reduces the b–c genetic distance by 54.6% and the c–px genetic distance by 92.4%, compared with control crosses between b c px and Oregon-R (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 1.

claim: All recombinants with both Sd and In(2R)Mal show strong drive.
source: Our crosses confirm that In(2R)Mal is indeed required for drive: if we generate recombinants along an SD-Mal chromosome, all recombinants with both Sd and In(2R)Mal show strong drive (Table 2, rows 1 and 2)
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 2.

claim: None of the recombinants that separate Sd and In(2R)Mal drive.
source: Our crosses confirm that In(2R)Mal is indeed required for drive: if we generate recombinants along an SD-Mal chromosome, all recombinants with both Sd and In(2R)Mal show strong drive (Table 2, rows 1 and 2), whereas none of the recombinants that separate Sd and In(2R)Mal drive (Table 2, rows 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 2.

claim: SD-Mal drive requires both Sd and In(2R)Mal.
source: We conclude that SD-Mal drive requires both Sd and In(2R)Mal, which implies that one or more essential enhancers, or co-drivers, is located within or distal to In(2R)Mal.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic crosses showing that both components are necessary for drive.

claim: One or more essential enhancers, or co-drivers, is located within or distal to In(2R)Mal.
source: We conclude that SD-Mal drive requires both Sd and In(2R)Mal, which implies that one or more essential enhancers, or co-drivers, is located within or distal to In(2R)Mal.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of both Sd and In(2R)Mal for drive.

claim: All b+ Sd c+ In(2R)Mal px recombinants show strong drive (n = 71).
source: To distinguish these possibilities, we measured drive in b+ Sd c+ In(2R)Mal px recombinants, which bear Sd and In(2R)Mal but have recombined between the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal (2R:18,774,475) and px (2R:22,494,297). All of these recombinants show strong drive (n = 71; Table 2, row 2).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 2.

claim: The probability of failing to separate an essential co-driver or distal enhancer among 71 recombinants is <0.014, assuming uniform recombination distribution.
source: Assuming that recombination is uniformly distributed throughout the 3.72 Mb interval between the In(2R)Mal-d distal breakpoint and px, the probability of failing to separate an essential co-driver or distal enhancer among any of our 71 recombinants is <0.014.
evidence: This is a statistical calculation based on the recombination data.

claim: Two recombinants within 100 kb of the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal both have strong drive (k > 0.99).
source: Furthermore, using molecular markers (see Materials and methods), we detected two recombinants within 100 kb of the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal, both with strong drive (k > 0.99; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on molecular marker analysis and drive measurements.

claim: The co-driver resides inside or within 100 kb of the In(2R)Mal arrangement.
source: We therefore infer that the co-driver resides inside or within 100 kb of the In(2R)Mal arrangement.
evidence: This is inferred from the recombination and drive data.

claim: The In(2R)Mal-d inversion both captured the co-driver and reduced recombination with Sd.
source: More specifically, we speculate that the In(2R)Mal-d inversion both captured the co-driver and reduced recombination with Sd, whereas In(2R)Mal-p tightened linkage between centromere-proximal components of SD-Mal and In(2R)Mal-d.
evidence: This is speculation based on the temporal order of inversions and their effects.

claim: In(2R)Mal-p tightened linkage between centromere-proximal components of SD-Mal and In(2R)Mal-d.
source: More specifically, we speculate that the In(2R)Mal-d inversion both captured the co-driver and reduced recombination with Sd, whereas In(2R)Mal-p tightened linkage between centromere-proximal components of SD-Mal and In(2R)Mal-d.
evidence: This is speculation based on the temporal order of inversions and their effects.

claim: Recombination occurs readily between Sd and the proximal break of In(2R)Mal.
source: Despite the recruitment of these inversions, recombination occurs readily between Sd and the proximal break of In(2R)Mal (Table 2; Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: Among 204 haploid genomes from Zambia, there were 198 wildtype haplotypes (Sd+ In(2R)Mal+), 3 SD-Mal haplotypes (Sd In(2R)Mal), and 3 recombinant haplotypes (three Sd In(2R)Mal+, zero Sd+ In(2R)Mal).
source: Among 204 haploid genomes from Zambia (Lack et al., 2016; see Materials and methods), we identified 198 wildtype haplotypes (Sd+ In(2R)Mal+), 3 SD-Mal haplotypes (Sd In(2R)Mal), and 3 recombinant haplotypes (three Sd In(2R)Mal+, zero Sd+ In(2R)Mal).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from Lack et al., 2016.

claim: Sd and In(2R)Mal have individually low sample frequencies (0.0294 and 0.0147, respectively) but tend to co-occur on the same chromosome (r2 = 0.493; Fisher's exact p = 1.4 × 10–5).
source: While Sd and In(2R)Mal each have individually low sample frequencies (0.0294 and 0.0147, respectively), they tend to co-occur on the same chromosome (r2 = 0.493; Fisher's exact p = 1.4 × 10–5).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the genomic data.

claim: The observed estimated coefficient of linkage disequilibrium between Sd and In(2R)Mal, D = 0.0143, has an expected half-life of just ~28 generations (2.8 years) in the absence of selection.
source: We calculated the expected decay of linkage disequilibrium between Sd and In(2R)Mal in the absence of any natural selection (Hill and Robertson, 1968), assuming a conservative sex-averaged recombination frequency corresponding to a map distance between Sd and In(2R)Mal of ~2.5 cM (FlyBase; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021) and an effective population size of 106. Under these assumptions, the observed estimated coefficient of linkage disequilibrium, D = 0.0143, has an expected half-life of just ~28 generations (2.8 years)
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations using the Hill and Robertson, 1968 model and data from FlyBase.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium between Sd and In(2R)Mal decays to negligible levels (expected D and r2 both ~10–3) in <100 generations (<10 years) in the absence of selection.
source: We calculated the expected decay of linkage disequilibrium between Sd and In(2R)Mal in the absence of any natural selection (Hill and Robertson, 1968), assuming a conservative sex-averaged recombination frequency corresponding to a map distance between Sd and In(2R)Mal of ~2.5 cM (FlyBase; FB2021_06; Larkin et al., 2021) and an effective population size of 106. Under these assumptions, the observed estimated coefficient of linkage disequilibrium, D = 0.0143, has an expected half-life of just ~28 generations (2.8 years) and, decays to negligible levels (i.e., expected D and r2 both ~10–3) in <100 generations (<10 years).
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations using the Hill and Robertson, 1968 model.

claim: The SD-Mal supergene haplotype is maintained by strong epistatic selection.
source: We therefore conclude that the SD-Mal supergene haplotype is maintained by strong epistatic selection.
evidence: This is concluded from the observed long-range linkage disequilibrium that would decay rapidly without selection.

claim: Nucleotide diversity (π) is significantly lower on SD-Mal haplotypes compared to uninverted SD+ chromosome arms.
source: Table 3 shows that nucleotide diversity (π) is significantly lower on SD-Mal haplotypes compared to uninverted SD+ chromosome arms (Table 3; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Table 3 and Figure 2A.

claim: The relative reduction in diversity on SD-Mal haplotypes extends from Sd-RanGAP on 2L across the centromere to ~2.9 Mb beyond the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal, spanning ~25.8 Mb (53% of chromosome 2).
source: The relative reduction in diversity on SD-Mal haplotypes is distributed heterogeneously: π is sharply reduced for a large region that spans ~25.8 Mb, representing 53% of chromosome 2 and extending from Sd-RanGAP on 2L (2L:19,441,959; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), across the centromere, and to ~2.9 Mb beyond the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal (2R:18,774,475; Table 3, rows 3, 5, and 6; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Table 3 and Figure 2A.

claim: The region of reduced nucleotide diversity on SD-Mal chromosomes covers all the known essential loci for the drive phenotype: Sd-RanGAP, Rspi, and In(2R)Mal.
source: Thus, the region of reduced nucleotide diversity on SD-Mal chromosomes covers all the known essential loci for the drive phenotype: Sd-RanGAP, Rspi, and In(2R)Mal.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the diversity analysis.

claim: SD-Mal frequency in Zambia was estimated to be 1.47% by identifying the Sd duplication and In(2R)Mal breakpoints in 204 haploid genomes.
source: We estimated SD-Mal frequency to be 1.47% by identifying the Sd duplication and In(2R)Mal breakpoints in 204 haploid genomes from Zambia (3/204, comparable to Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015; data from Lack et al., 2016; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from Lack et al., 2016 and is comparable to previous estimates.

claim: Nucleotide diversity outside of the SD-Mal supergene region is comparable to SD+.
source: While nucleotide diversity outside of the SD-Mal supergene region is comparable to SD+ (Table 3, row 1)
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: Diversity in the SD-Mal supergene region is significantly lower than expected even when scaled by its frequency (1.47%).
source: diversity in the supergene region is significantly lower than expected even when scaled by its frequency (Table 3, row 4), suggesting that the low population frequency of SD-Mal cannot fully explain its reduced diversity.
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: SD-Mal shows strongly negative Tajima's D, indicating an excess of rare alleles.
source: We find strongly negative Tajima's D mirroring the distribution of reduced diversity, indicating an excess of rare alleles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The skew in the site frequency spectrum suggests a recent increase in frequency of the SD-Mal supergene in Zambia.
source: Such a skew in the site frequency spectrum suggests a recent increase in frequency of the SD-Mal supergene in Zambia.
evidence: This is inferred from the strongly negative Tajima's D.

claim: FST in the SD-Mal supergene region is unusually high for chromosomes from the same population.
source: FST in the SD-Mal supergene region is unusually high for chromosomes from the same population (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither of the SD+ chromosomes with cosmopolitan inversions show such high differentiation as SD-Mal.
source: Neither of the SD+ chromosomes with cosmopolitan inversions show such high differentiation, and mean nucleotide differences (dXY) between SD-Mal and SD+ are comparable to the other inversions, implying that the differentiation of the SD-Mal supergene is recent.
evidence: This is based on population genomic analysis comparing FST and dXY values.

claim: Mean nucleotide differences (dXY) between SD-Mal and SD+ are comparable to the other inversions, implying that the differentiation of the SD-Mal supergene is recent.
source: Neither of the SD+ chromosomes with cosmopolitan inversions show such high differentiation, and mean nucleotide differences (dXY) between SD-Mal and SD+ are comparable to the other inversions, implying that the differentiation of the SD-Mal supergene is recent.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dXY values.

claim: The results—low diversity, strongly negative Tajima's D, high FST and relatively low dXY—are consistent with a rapid increase in frequency of the SD-Mal haplotype.
source: Our results—low diversity, strongly negative Tajima's D, high FST and relatively low dXY—are thus consistent with a rapid increase in frequency of the SD-Mal haplotype that reduced nucleotide diversity within SD-Mal and generated large differences in allele frequencies with SD+ chromosomes (e.g., Charlesworth, 1998; Cruickshank and Hahn, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the population genomic patterns and supported by citations to Charlesworth, 1998 and Cruickshank and Hahn, 2014.

claim: The SD-Mal expansion began ~0.0884 (95% CIs 0.0837–0.1067) × 4Ne generations ago or ~1644 years ago, based on all SNPs.
source: Using the ABC with rejection sampling conditional on our observed estimates of π and Tajima's D for In(2R)Mal (πIn(2R)Mal = 584.60, D = –1.33; note that πIn(2R)Mal is an overall, unscaled estimate of nucleotide diversity for the whole In(2R)Mal region and that only non-coding regions were considered), we infer that the SD-Mal expansion began ~0.0884 (95% CIs 0.0837–0.1067) × 4Ne generations ago or, equivalently, ~1644 years ago (1.11% rejection sampling acceptance rate; Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on ABC simulations and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Based on private SNPs only, the estimated SD-Mal expansion occurred ~0.0679 (95% CIs 0.0647–0.0868) 4Ne generations ago, ~1261 years.
source: To account for possible effects of gene conversion between SD and SD+ chromosomes (see below), we discarded SNPs shared with SD+ chromosomes (see below), and recalculated π and Tajima's D using only private SNPs (πIn(2R)Mal = 427.72, D = –1.45). Based on these parameters, the estimated SD-Mal expansion occurred ~0.0679 (95% CIs 0.0647–0.0868) 4Ne generations ago, ~1261 years (1.02% rejection sampling acceptance rate; Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on ABC simulations using only private SNPs and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The simulated data are inconsistent with a long-term stable frequency of SD-Mal.
source: The simulated data are inconsistent with a long-term stable frequency of SD-Mal (all SNPs, pπ = 0.0522, pD = 0.096; private, pπ = 0.0266, pD = 0.0668)
evidence: This is based on posterior probability calculations from simulations.

claim: The simulated data are inconsistent with long-term exponential growth of SD-Mal.
source: or long-term exponential growth (all SNPs, pπ = 0.0465, pD = 0.0907; private, pπ = 0.0215, pD = 0.0605).
evidence: This is based on posterior probability calculations from simulations.

claim: A recent selective sweep is more consistent with the data than stable frequency or exponential growth models.
source: Instead, our simulations suggest that a recent selective sweep is more consistent with the data (all SNPs, pπ = 0.3554, pD = 0.5952; private, pπ = 0.3480, pD = 0.6142).
evidence: This is based on posterior probability calculations from simulations.

claim: Evidence from nucleotide diversity, the site frequency spectrum, population differentiation, and coalescent simulations suggests a rapid non-neutral increase in frequency of the SD-Mal supergene that began <2000 years ago.
source: Taken together, evidence from nucleotide diversity, the site frequency spectrum, population differentiation, and coalescent simulations suggests a rapid non-neutral increase in frequency of the SD-Mal supergene that began <2000 years ago.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The sweep signal on the SD-Mal haplotypes begins immediately distal to Sd-RanGAP on 2L and extends ~3 Mb beyond the distal boundary of In(2R)Mal on 2R.
source: The sweep signal on the SD-Mal haplotypes begins immediately distal to Sd-RanGAP on 2L and extends ~3 Mb beyond the distal boundary of In(2R)Mal on 2R.
evidence: This is based on the population genomic analysis of diversity and Tajima's D.

claim: Chromosomal inversions can suppress recombination ~1–3 Mb beyond their breakpoints.
source: First, chromosomal inversions can suppress recombination ~1–3 Mb beyond their breakpoints (in both multiply inverted balancer chromosomes, [Miller et al., 2016; Crown et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2018] and natural inversions [Stevison et al., 2011; Fuller et al., 2017]), extending the size of the sweep signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2016; Crown et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2018; Stevison et al., 2011; Fuller et al., 2017.

claim: The expected genetic distance between the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal (2R:18.77 Mb) and px (2R:22.49 Mb) is ~13.87 cM.
source: The expected genetic distance between the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal (2R:18.77 Mb) and px (2R:22.49 Mb) is ~13.87 cM (Fiston-Lavier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fiston-Lavier et al., 2010.

claim: Measuring recombination between SD-Mal and standard arrangement chromosomes for the interval between the distal breakpoint of In(2R)Mal and px, the genetic distance is ~1.76 cM, an 87.3% reduction.
source: Measuring recombination between SD-Mal and standard arrangement chromosomes for the same (collinear) interval, we estimate a genetic distance of ~1.76 (Table 1), an 87.3% reduction.
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 1.

claim: In(2R)Mal strongly reduces recombination beyond its distal boundary.
source: In(2R)Mal strongly reduces recombination beyond its distal boundary.
evidence: This is concluded from the measured reduction in genetic distance.

claim: SD-Mal chromosomes with In(2R)Mal-distal material recombined away (b+ Sd c+ In(2R)Mal px) have modestly but significantly lower drive strength (k = 0.96 vs. 0.98) than those without recombination.
source: We find that SD-Mal chromosomes with In(2R)Mal-distal material recombined away (b+ Sd c+ In(2R)Mal px) have modestly but significantly lower drive strength (k = 0.96 vs. 0.98; Table 2, lines 1–2), suggestive of one or more weak distal enhancers.
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and data presented in Table 2.

claim: The modest reduction in drive strength in recombinants is suggestive of one or more weak distal enhancers.
source: We find that SD-Mal chromosomes with In(2R)Mal-distal material recombined away (b+ Sd c+ In(2R)Mal px) have modestly but significantly lower drive strength (k = 0.96 vs. 0.98; Table 2, lines 1–2), suggestive of one or more weak distal enhancers.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed modest reduction in drive strength.

claim: Most supergenes show long-range LD, reduced nucleotide diversity, and differentiation when compared with their wildtype counterparts.
source: Most supergenes show long-range LD, reduced nucleotide diversity, and differentiation when compared with their wildtype counterparts.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about supergenes.

claim: Some meiotic drive supergenes show evidence of recurrent selective sweeps.
source: While some meiotic drive supergenes show evidence of recurrent selective sweeps (Dyer et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dyer et al., 2007.

claim: Some meiotic drive supergenes show a signature of epistatic selection without strong selective sweeps.
source: or a signature of epistatic selection without strong selective sweeps (Fuller et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fuller et al., 2020.

claim: Some meiotic drive supergenes show no signatures of recent or ongoing positive selection.
source: others show no signatures of recent or ongoing positive selection (Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018.

claim: The relatively recent origin (~38.5 kya) of SD might explain the constant turnover, as there may not have been enough time to reach a stable equilibrium compared to older drive systems like the t-haplotype.
source: The relatively recent origin (~38.5 kya; Brand et al., 2015) of SD might explain the constant turnover, as there may not have been enough time to reach a stable equilibrium compared to older drive systems like the t-haplotype, whose first inversion arose 3 mya (Hammer and Silver, 1993).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Brand et al., 2015 and Hammer and Silver, 1993.

claim: The t-haplotype's first inversion arose 3 mya.
source: The relatively recent origin (~38.5 kya; Brand et al., 2015) of SD might explain the constant turnover, as there may not have been enough time to reach a stable equilibrium compared to older drive systems like the t-haplotype, whose first inversion arose 3 mya (Hammer and Silver, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hammer and Silver, 1993.

claim: Nearly all SD-Mal haplotypes are individually homozygous lethal.
source: While nearly all SD-Mal haplotypes are individually homozygous lethal and do not recombine with wildtype chromosomes in and around In(2R)Mal
evidence: This is stated as a fact about SD-Mal haplotypes.

claim: ~90% of pairwise combinations of different SD-Mal chromosomes (SDi/SDj) are viable and fertile in complementation tests.
source: ~90% of pairwise combinations of different SD-Mal chromosomes (SDi/SDj) are viable and fertile in complementation tests (Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: Mean pairwise linkage disequilibrium (r2) between SNPs located within the In(2R)Mal arrangement declines as a function of the physical distance separating them.
source: To determine if SD-Mal chromosomes recombine, we estimated mean pairwise linkage disequilibrium (r2) between SNPs located within the In(2R)Mal arrangement. We found that mean r2 between pairs of SNPs declines as a function of the physical distance separating them (Figure 5A), a hallmark of recombination via crossing over (Hill and Robertson, 1968; Miyashita and Langley, 1988; Schaeffer and Miller, 1993; Awadalla et al., 1999; Conway et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on LD analysis shown in Figure 5A and supported by citations to Hill and Robertson, 1968; Miyashita and Langley, 1988; Schaeffer and Miller, 1993; Awadalla et al., 1999; Conway et al., 1999.

claim: The decline of mean r2 with physical distance is a hallmark of recombination via crossing over.
source: We found that mean r2 between pairs of SNPs declines as a function of the physical distance separating them (Figure 5A), a hallmark of recombination via crossing over (Hill and Robertson, 1968; Miyashita and Langley, 1988; Schaeffer and Miller, 1993; Awadalla et al., 1999; Conway et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hill and Robertson, 1968; Miyashita and Langley, 1988; Schaeffer and Miller, 1993; Awadalla et al., 1999; Conway et al., 1999.

claim: Pairwise LD is higher and extends further in In(2R)Mal than in the equivalent region of SD+ chromosomes or in any of the other two cosmopolitan inversions, In(2L)t and In(2R)NS.
source: Pairwise LD is higher and extends further in In(2R)Mal than in the equivalent region of SD+ chromosomes or in any of the other two cosmopolitan inversions, In(2L)t and In(2R)NS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on LD analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The minimum number of recombination events (Rm) in the sample of SD-Mal haplotypes is 15, based on 338 non-singleton, biallelic SNPs in In(2R)Mal.
source: To further characterize the history of recombination between SD-Mal haplotypes, we used 338 non-singleton, biallelic SNPs in In(2R)Mal to trace historical crossover events. From these SNPs, we estimate that Rm (Hudson and Kaplan, 1985), the minimum number of recombination events, in this sample of SD-Mal haplotypes is 15 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on analysis using the method from Hudson and Kaplan, 1985 and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Recombination events between SD-Mal haplotypes occur a minimum of once every ~1096 generations, assuming SD-Mal haplotypes are ~16,436 generations old.
source: Thus, assuming that these SD-Mal haplotypes are ~16,436 generations old (Figure 4), we estimate that recombination events between SD-Mal haplotypes occur a minimum of once every ~1096 generations.
evidence: This is calculated from the minimum number of recombination events and the estimated age of SD-Mal.

claim: Crossover events between SD-Mal haplotypes are relatively rare, likely due to the low population frequency of SD-Mal and the possibly reduced fitness of SDi/SDj genotypes.
source: We can thus confirm that crossover events are relatively rare, likely due to the low population frequency of SD-Mal and the possibly reduced fitness of SDi/SDj genotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the low frequency of recombination events.

claim: In In(2R)Mal, SNP density is five times higher for runs of shared SNPs (0.63 SNPs/kb) than for runs of SD-private SNPs (0.12 SNPs/kb).
source: Accordingly, in In(2R)Mal, SNP density is five times higher for runs of shared SNPs (0.63 SNPs/kb) than for runs of SD-private SNPs (0.12 SNPs/kb), as expected if SD+ chromosomes, which have higher SNP densities, were donors of conversion tract sequences.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNP density in shared vs. private SNP runs.

claim: 62.2% (89 out of 143) of the shared SNP runs are <1 kb.
source: Although we cannot exclude the contribution of double crossovers, we note that 62.2% (89 out of 143) of the shared SNP runs are <1 kb, 80.4% (115 out of 143) are <10 kb (Figure 5B), and the longest run is ~50.2 kb.
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared SNP run lengths shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 80.4% (115 out of 143) of the shared SNP runs are <10 kb.
source: Although we cannot exclude the contribution of double crossovers, we note that 62.2% (89 out of 143) of the shared SNP runs are <1 kb, 80.4% (115 out of 143) are <10 kb (Figure 5B), and the longest run is ~50.2 kb.
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared SNP run lengths shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The longest shared SNP run is ~50.2 kb.
source: Although we cannot exclude the contribution of double crossovers, we note that 62.2% (89 out of 143) of the shared SNP runs are <1 kb, 80.4% (115 out of 143) are <10 kb (Figure 5B), and the longest run is ~50.2 kb.
evidence: This is based on analysis of shared SNP run lengths.

claim: The sizes of shared SNP runs are more consistent with current estimates of gene conversion tract lengths in D. melanogaster than with double cross-overs.
source: These sizes are more consistent with current estimates of gene conversion tract lengths in D. melanogaster than with double cross-overs (Comeron et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Comeron et al., 2012 and Miller et al., 2016.

claim: Inferred gene conversion events are unevenly distributed across In(2R)Mal, being more frequent in the In(2R)Mal-p than in In(2R)Mal-d.
source: Surprisingly, these inferred gene conversion events are unevenly distributed across In(2R)Mal, being more frequent in the In(2R)Mal-p than in In(2R)Mal-d (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the distribution of shared SNPs.

claim: SD-Mal haplotypes can recombine with each other, distinguishing the SD-Mal supergene from supergenes that are completely genetically isolated.
source: Our discovery that SD-Mal haplotypes can recombine with each other distinguishes the SD-Mal supergene from supergenes that are completely genetically isolated (Wang et al., 2013; Charlesworth, 2016; Tuttle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is concluded from the recombination analysis and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2013; Charlesworth, 2016; Tuttle et al., 2016.

claim: SD-Mal haplotypes evolve as a semi-isolated subpopulation, with a nearly 100-fold smaller Ne and limited gene flow from SD+ via gene conversion events.
source: The lack of crossing over with SD+ chromosomes, however, means that SD-Mal haplotypes evolve as a semi-isolated subpopulation, with a nearly 100-fold smaller Ne and limited gene flow from SD+ via gene conversion events.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of crossing over with SD+ and the observed gene conversion.

claim: For the SNPs in In(2R)Mal, the overall N/S ratio is 2.3-fold higher than that for the same region of SD+ chromosomes.
source: For the SNPs in In(2R)Mal, the overall N/S ratio is 2.3-fold higher than that for the same region of SD+ chromosomes (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNPs shown in Table 4.

claim: The N/S ratio for private SNPs in In(2R)Mal is 3.1-fold higher than for SD+ chromosomes.
source: Notably, the N/S ratio for private SNPs is 3.1-fold higher (Table 4)
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNPs shown in Table 4.

claim: The N/S ratios for shared SNPs do not significantly differ from SD+ chromosomes.
source: whereas the N/S ratios for shared SNPs do not significantly differ from SD+ chromosomes (Table 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNPs shown in Table 4 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene conversion from SD+ ameliorates the accumulation of potentially deleterious non-synonymous mutations on SD-Mal chromosomes.
source: These findings suggest that gene conversion from SD+ ameliorates the accumulation of potentially deleterious non-synonymous mutations on SD-Mal chromosomes (see also Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018; Pieper and Dyer, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in N/S ratios between shared and private SNPs, and supported by citations to Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018 and Pieper and Dyer, 2016.

claim: TEs accumulate in regions of reduced recombination, such as centromeres and inversions, especially those at low frequency.
source: TEs accumulate in regions of reduced recombination, such as centromeres (Charlesworth et al., 1994) and inversions, especially those at low frequency (Eanes et al., 2009; Sniegowski and Charlesworth, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Charlesworth et al., 1994; Eanes et al., 2009; Sniegowski and Charlesworth, 1994.

claim: TE densities for the whole euchromatic region of chromosome 2R are significantly higher for SD-Mal compared to SD+ chromosomes.
source: Indeed, TE densities for the whole euchromatic region of chromosome 2R are significantly higher for SD-Mal compared to SD+ chromosomes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on TE analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increased TE density on SD-Mal is driven by the low recombination regions of the haplotype: In(2R)Mal has significantly higher TE density than SD+ whereas the distal region of 2R outside of the sweep region does not.
source: This increased TE density on SD-Mal is driven by the low recombination regions of the haplotype: In(2R)Mal has significantly higher TE density than SD+ whereas the distal region of 2R outside of the sweep region does not (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on TE analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The most overrepresented TE families in In(2R)Mal relative to standard chromosomes are M4DM, MDG1, ROO_I, and LINE elements.
source: The most overrepresented families in In(2R)Mal relative to standard chromosomes are M4DM, MDG1, ROO_I, and LINE elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)—TEs that are currently or recently active (Kaminker et al., 2002; Kofler et al., 2015; Diaz-González and Dominguez, 2020)—consistent with the recent origin of the SD-Mal haplotype.
evidence: This is based on TE analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations to Kaminker et al., 2002; Kofler et al., 2015; Diaz-González and Dominguez, 2020.

claim: M4DM, MDG1, ROO_I, and LINE elements are currently or recently active TEs.
source: The most overrepresented families in In(2R)Mal relative to standard chromosomes are M4DM, MDG1, ROO_I, and LINE elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)—TEs that are currently or recently active (Kaminker et al., 2002; Kofler et al., 2015; Diaz-González and Dominguez, 2020)—consistent with the recent origin of the SD-Mal haplotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaminker et al., 2002; Kofler et al., 2015; Diaz-González and Dominguez, 2020.

claim: The overrepresentation of currently or recently active TEs is consistent with the recent origin of the SD-Mal haplotype.
source: The most overrepresented families in In(2R)Mal relative to standard chromosomes are M4DM, MDG1, ROO_I, and LINE elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)—TEs that are currently or recently active (Kaminker et al., 2002; Kofler et al., 2015; Diaz-González and Dominguez, 2020)—consistent with the recent origin of the SD-Mal haplotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the TE composition and the recent origin of SD-Mal.

claim: The differences in shared vs. private SNPs suggests that gene conversion from SD+ chromosomes may slow the accumulation of deleterious point mutations but not the accumulation of TEs.
source: Thus, the differences in shared vs. private SNPs suggests that gene conversion from SD+ chromosomes may slow the accumulation of deleterious point mutations but not the accumulation of TEs.
evidence: This is inferred from the different patterns of N/S ratios and TE accumulation.

claim: Despite occasional recombination, the small Ne of SD-Mal haplotypes has incurred a higher genetic load.
source: Despite occasional recombination, the small Ne of SD-Mal haplotypes has incurred a higher genetic load.
evidence: This is concluded from the elevated N/S ratios and TE accumulation.

claim: The SD-Mal supergene extends across ~25.8 Mb of D. melanogaster chromosome 2, comprising the driving Sd-RanGAP, a drive-insensitive deletion at the major Rsp locus, and the In(2R)Mal double inversion.
source: Our findings demonstrate, first, that the SD-Mal supergene extends across ~25.8 Mb of D. melanogaster chromosome 2, a region that comprises the driving Sd-RanGAP, a drive-insensitive deletion at the major Rsp locus, and the In(2R)Mal double inversion.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: SD-Mal requires Sd-RanGAP and an essential co-driver that localizes almost certainly within the In(2R)Mal rearrangement, and probably within the distal inversion.
source: Second, using genetic manipulation, we show that SD-Mal requires Sd-RanGAP and an essential co-driver that localizes almost certainly within the In(2R)Mal rearrangement, and probably within the distal inversion.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from genetic crosses.

claim: There is experimental evidence for epistasis between Sd-RanGAP and In(2R)Mal: neither allele can drive without the other.
source: These data provide experimental evidence for epistasis between Sd-RanGAP and In(2R)Mal: neither allele can drive without the other.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic crosses showing both components are necessary for drive.

claim: Epistatic selection on loci spanning the SD-Mal supergene region drove a very recent, chromosome-scale selective sweep.
source: Third, we provide population genomics evidence that epistatic selection on loci spanning the SD-Mal supergene region drove a very recent, chromosome-scale selective sweep.
evidence: This is a summary of the population genomic findings.

claim: The population genomic patterns are consistent with recurrent episodes of replacement of one SD haplotype by others.
source: These patterns are consistent with recurrent episodes of replacement of one SD haplotype by others (Presgraves et al., 2009; Brand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the population genomic patterns and supported by citations to Presgraves et al., 2009 and Brand et al., 2015.

claim: Despite rare crossovers among complementing SD-Mal haplotypes and gene conversion from wildtype chromosomes, the relative genetic isolation and low frequency of SD-Mal results in the accumulation of deleterious mutations including, especially, TE insertions.
source: Fourth, despite rare crossovers among complementing SD-Mal haplotypes and gene conversion from wildtype chromosomes, the relative genetic isolation and low frequency of SD-Mal results in the accumulation of deleterious mutations including, especially, TE insertions.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on genetic load.

claim: The SD-Mal supergene population is of small effective size, semi-isolate from the greater population of wildtype chromosomes, and subject to bouts of very strong selection.
source: From these findings, we conclude that the SD-Mal supergene population is of small effective size, semi-isolate from the greater population of wildtype chromosomes, and subject to bouts of very strong selection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the findings.

claim: Non-recombining supergenes that exist exclusively in heterozygous state tend to degenerate, as in the case of Y chromosomes and some autosomal supergenes which lack any opportunity for recombination.
source: Non-recombining supergenes that exist exclusively in heterozygous state tend to degenerate, as in the case of Y chromosomes (reviewed in Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2000) and some autosomal supergenes which, for different reasons, lack any opportunity for recombination (Uyenoyama, 2005; Wang et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Branco et al., 2018; Stolle et al., 2019; Brelsford et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2000; Uyenoyama, 2005; Wang et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Branco et al., 2018; Stolle et al., 2019; Brelsford et al., 2020.

claim: Not all supergenes are necessarily expected to degenerate.
source: But not all supergenes are necessarily expected to degenerate.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the previous claim about degeneration.

claim: In the mouse t-haplotype, there is evidence for occasional recombination between complementing t-haplotypes and with standard chromosomes, probably via gene conversion.
source: In the mouse t-haplotype, there is similar evidence for occasional recombination between complementing t-haplotypes (Dod et al., 2003) and with standard chromosomes, probably via gene conversion (Herrmann et al., 1987; Erhart et al., 2002; Wallace and Erhart, 2008; Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dod et al., 2003; Herrmann et al., 1987; Erhart et al., 2002; Wallace and Erhart, 2008; Kelemen and Vicoso, 2018.

claim: Despite the many parallels characterizing supergenes, their ultimate evolutionary fates depend on the particulars of the system.
source: Despite the many parallels characterizing supergenes, their ultimate evolutionary fates depend on the particulars of the system.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about supergene evolution.
